detail.longDescription: A free lane is the wrong bet when you cannot reserve the attempt before anything admits it. A zero price does not make the prompt free of time, and a client timeout does not hand the tokens back. You already know the paid version of this failure. The call returns a transcript, the meter moves, and you argue with the bill after the fact. The free version only feels different because no invoice shows up. It is not different in the way that matters. Something still read the prompt, something still held a slot, and your next retry still starts from a smaller remainder than the dashboard in your head. Think of a counter that comps the drink and still makes you stand in line. The coupon changes who pays. It does not un-grind the beans if you walk out after the order was fired, and it does not give you the meeting you missed while you waited. Free model access works like that coupon. Useful, limited, and easy to misuse if you treat admission as a result. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. A free model path, and a free server option beside it, is a reasonable place to practice the habit below. It is not a committed slot, and this note does not pretend otherwise. What the attempt actually spends Every attempt spends four things, on a free lane or a paid one. It spends input when the prompt leaves your process. It spends output if generation actually starts. It spends wait between admit and the first usable token. It spends a second attempt if your client treats silence as "that never happened." The fourth spend is the leak. Your HTTP client gives up at 30 seconds. The server may still be generating, or still sitting in a queue whose clock you do not own. You retry because the spinner looked stuck. Now one user action owns two attempts, and you can merge at most one of them. Without an attempt id, you cannot even say which transcript belongs to which click. Free capacity makes the leak worse only because it feels safe to ignore. You tell yourself the duplicate was free. The duplicate still occupied the slot your real job needed, and it still burned the context you will not resend cheaply once the window is gone. Queue time was never a refundable deposit. Neither is a prompt that already left the building. Reserve before you are admitted The fix is dull, which is why it holds. Before you enqueue, estimate the input, reserve an output cap, and add a slack term for the wait you are willing to abandon. If that reservation does not fit in the job's remaining budget, you do not join the queue. You fail closed in your own process, where failure is still cheap. The sketch below is a proposal, not a measured run. It uses a character heuristic, not a vendor tokenizer. Swap in the tokenizer you actually ship before you trust a number. The control flow is the artifact: one reservation, one attempt id, no sibling call from a timeout. import hashlib import time from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class Budget: remaining_tokens: int max_wait_s: float max_attempts: int @dataclass class Attempt: attempt: str reserved: int deadline: float status: str # reserved | abandoned | done def estimate_tokens(text: str) -> int: # Stand-in only. Replace with the tokenizer for the model you call. return max(1, (len(text) + 3) // 4) def reserve(prompt: str, output_cap: int, slack_tokens: int) -> int: return estimate_tokens(prompt) + output_cap + slack_tokens def attempt_id(job_id: str, prompt: str, n: int) -> str: raw = f"{job_id}|{n}|{prompt}".encode() return hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()[:16] def admit(job_id, prompt, budget, output_cap, slack, n): need = reserve(prompt, output_cap, slack) if n >= budget.max_attempts or need > budget.remaining_tokens: return {"action": "refuse", "need": need, "remaining": budget.remaining_tokens} budget.remaining_tokens -= need att = Attempt( attempt=attempt_id(job_id, prompt, n), reserved=need, deadline=time.time() + budget.max_wait_s, status="reserved", ) return {"action": "enqueue", "attempt": att} def on_timeout(att: Attempt, budget: Budget): # Silence is not a new job. Do not call admit() from this branch. att.status = "abandoned" return {"action": "stop", "attempt": att.attempt, "remaining": budget.remaining_tokens} def on_usage(att: Attempt, budget: Budget, actual: int): # Give back unused reserve, or eat the overage if the estimate lied. delta = att.reserved - actual budget.remaining_tokens += delta att.status = "done" return {"action": "reconcile", "delta": delta, "remaining": budget.remaining_tokens} You call admit once per user action, not once per socket error. If it returns refuse , you stop. You do not "just try the free server and see." Seeing is the spend. A timeout calls on_timeout and leaves the attempt id alone. A later response, if one still arrives, reconciles against that same id. It does not open a second reservation. python - <<'PY' from pathlib import Path # paste the sketch above, then: b = Budget(remaining_tokens=1200, max_wait_s=20, max_attempts=1) prompt = Path("prompt.txt").read_text() first = admit("job-19", prompt, b, output_cap=400, slack=200, n=0) print(first["action"]) if first["action"] == "enqueue": print(on_timeout(first["attempt"], b)["action"]) second = admit("job-19", prompt, b, output_cap=400, slack=200, n=1) print(second["action"], second["remaining"]) PY Read that as a spec, not as a benchmark. The first call may enqueue and subtract the reserve. The timeout marks that attempt abandoned and does not refund the wait you already chose to risk. The second call should refuse, because max_attempts is 1. If your production client does the opposite — retry on timeout, then retry on disconnect, then retry because the UI looked frozen — you have rebuilt the leak in three places, and a free lane will not save you from it. Slack is the part people set to zero and then regret. Some of the reservation is not tokens you expect to see in a usage field. It is the cost of being wrong about wait. If you cannot name a number you are willing to abandon, you do not have a budget. You have a hope that the queue will be kind. Where an unknown wait belongs A free server option is a lane with an unknown wait, not a discount you sprinkle on every call. Use it for work that already has a refuse path. Batch labeling you can defer. A doc summary nobody is staring at. A fixture rebuild that can miss this hour. Put the same reservation in front of that lane that you would put in front of a paid one. The numbers in the budget change. The shape does not. Do not park a release gate there. A pipeline that must go green before you tag a build cannot wait-and-see on a queue you do not schedule. Do not park an interactive path there either, unless you are willing to show a refusal instead of a spinner. A spinner that hides a second attempt is how one click becomes two spends and one angry refresh. If the path you need is a guaranteed slot, a named quota, or a latency you can put in an SLO, stop. This workflow will not grow those properties out of a free option. Operator-supplied availability is not a capacity plan. Treat any free model route, including one you might try in MonkeyCode, as optional capacity for jobs that are allowed to miss. Who should skip the sketch Skip it when the call is single-shot, tiny, and already capped by a gateway you trust. A 200-token classification that cannot retry does not need a second budget object wrapped around it. Skip it when you cannot estimate input size at all. A reservation built on a lie is just a new surprise with extra steps. Skip it when the job is allowed to block a person. Blocking work needs a committed lane and a cancel the server actually honors. A local deadline field is not a cancel, and abandoning the attempt in your process does not prove the other side stopped reading. The heuristic will drift. Tool output, images, and a retried prefix blow past len(text)//4 . Use the estimate as a gate, then reconcile with on_usage when a usage field comes back. If the response has no usage field, you are flying on the reservation alone, so the cap gets stricter, not looser. Do not "fix" a missing usage field by raising max_attempts . That is the leak again, wearing a config flag. There is a second failure mode the sketch does not solve. Two workers can admit the same job_id if they do not share the Budget . A process-local counter is enough for a single client and a single job. It is not a distributed lock. If you fan out, the remaining-token number has to live where all of those callers can decrement it, or you will reserve the same tokens twice and call it parallelism. The habit worth keeping You do not win this by hunting a cheaper name on a model list. You win it by refusing to enqueue an attempt you have not reserved, and by refusing to mint a new attempt when the old one merely went quiet. Free capacity is a fine place to practice that, because a refusal there costs you a dropped job instead of a surprise invoice. It is a bad place to bet a deadline you cannot miss. Start with one droppable job. Keep max_attempts at 1. Log the refuse branch next to the enqueue branch, and do not celebrate a spinner that never printed stop . If the refuse count is zero for a week, your cap is decorative, and the queue is still spending prompts you never agreed to reserve. # devops # python # ai # tutorial # software # coding # development # engineering # inclusive # community Don't Enqueue What You Cannot Reserve
